t: The Jadids, who called themselves progressives, intellectuals or simply youth, held that Muslim peoples in Tsarist Russia had fallen into moral and societal decay that only a new kind of knowledge and European-modelled reform could cure.

Their signature was the Usul-i Jadid, the new method of teaching, which added geography, history, mathematics and science to the maktab curriculum, taught reading by phonetic methods and spread through schools and a Turkic-language press.
Their rivals were the Qadimist clergy and, after 1917, the Bolsheviks, who first used them and then purged them as counterrevolutionary agents; Uzbekistan has since honoured them as national heroes.
dyk: A Samarqand bookstore of 1914 sold books in Tatar, Ottoman, Arabic and Persian, along with dictionaries, atlases, maps and globes, according to the historian Adeeb Khalid.
ev: Ismail Gaspirali founds the first new-method school in Crimea
The 1905 Revolution opens a period in which Turkic-language newspapers appear in Turkestan; Russian authorities forbid them again in 1908
A school for training teachers in Jadid methods is founded in Turfan by Heyder Sayrani and the merchant Mukhsut Muhiti
Jadid-run institutions of learning number over 5,000
Jadids found a provisional government at Kokand, which the Tashkent Soviet crushes in 1918, killing around 14,000 people
The Communist Party in Central Asia turns on the Jadids in the same purges that struck the Ulama
Virtually the entire intelligentsia of Central Asia, including Cholpan and Abdurrauf Fitrat, is purged

f.where: The Russian Empire's Muslim and Turkic regions: Crimea, Tatarstan, Bashkortostan, the North Caucasus and Central Asia (Turkestan, Tashkent, Samarqand, Bukhara, Kokand), with echoes in Xinjiang.
f.period: The first new-method school in Crimea (1884); new-method schools appearing in the last decade of the 19th century; a burst of Turkic newspapers after the 1905 Revolution until 1908; over 5,000 Jadid schools by 1916; the Kokand government (1917–1918); alliance with the Bolsheviks in the early 1920s; purges from 1926 through the 1920s and 1930s.
f.figures: Ismail Gasprinsky (Gaspirali), Crimean Tatar educator and publisher; Mahmud Khoja Behbudiy, playwright and school founder; Abdurrauf Fitrat; Cholpan; Munawwar Qari; Sadriddin Ayni; Musa Bigiev; Ghabdennasir Qursawi; Zaynulla Rasulev.
f.outcome: A network of new-method schools and a Turkic-language press, but no equality under Russian rule; the Kokand government was crushed in 1917–1918, and the Jadids were purged under Stalin. They have since been rehabilitated as national heroes in Uzbekistan.
